title: Built-in Utility Types
summary: Build patches, create inputs, summaries, and lookup tables from one type with Partial, Omit, Pick, Record, Exclude, ReturnType, and more.
intro: One kind of data takes many shapes in a codebase: the full record, a patch that changes a few fields, the input a create function takes, the summary a list shows. Written by hand, those shapes drift apart the first time the record changes. TypeScript ships utility types, generic types that build each shape from the one type you already have, so a change to the original reaches all of them.

steps.title: Partial, Required, and Readonly

examples.title: Patches with Partial
examples.prompt: Update a user with a patch that holds only the fields that change.

examples.title: Defaults with Required
examples.prompt: Fill in the settings a user left out, and return a type where nothing is missing.
examples.explanation: `Settings` is what a user saves, so every field is optional. `Required<Settings>` removes every `?`, and as the return type it promises all three fields. Leave one out of the returned object and `tsc` reports which one is missing. After the call, `settings.fontSize` is a plain `number`, as the bubble shows, so the code that uses it needs no `?? 16` of its own.

examples.title: Readonly config
examples.prompt: Freeze a config object, then try to change its port.
examples.output: main.ts(5,8): error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'port' because it is a read-only property.
examples.explanation: `Readonly<Config>` marks both properties `readonly`, so `tsc` rejects the assignment on line 5, before anything runs. Delete that line and the program prints `localhost:8080`. The type and `Object.freeze` do different jobs: the type stops the code `tsc` checks, and `Object.freeze` makes the object itself refuse changes while the program runs.

practice.title: Apply a patch
practice.prompt:
Write a function that applies a patch to a product, then patch a mug twice.

1. Change the type of `patch` to `Partial<Product>`, so it accepts any subset of a product's fields.
2. Make `applyPatch` return a new product: the fields of `p`, overwritten by the fields in `patch`.
3. Apply `{ priceCents: 999 }` to `mug`, then `{ stock: 0 }` to the result, and print the product after each patch with `show`.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests call `applyPatch`.

Expected output:

```text
MUG-01 Mug: $12.99, 4 in stock
MUG-01 Mug: $9.99, 4 in stock
MUG-01 Mug: $9.99, 0 in stock
```

tests.output:
MUG-01 Mug: $12.99, 4 in stock
MUG-01 Mug: $9.99, 4 in stock
MUG-01 Mug: $9.99, 0 in stock

cases.name: accepts a patch with one field
cases.code:
declare const p: Product;
applyPatch(p, { priceCents: 100 });

cases.name: accepts an empty patch and returns a Product
cases.code:
declare const p: Product;
const same: Product = applyPatch(p, {});

cases.name: rejects a field Product doesn't have
cases.code:
declare const p: Product;
applyPatch(p, { colour: "red" });

cases.name: rejects a price that is a string
cases.code:
declare const p: Product;
applyPatch(p, { priceCents: "100" });

hints: `updateUser` in the first example does the same job for users. Compare its `patch` parameter with this one.
Spread both objects into a new one, `p` first, so the fields in `patch` win.

steps.title: Pick, Omit, and Record for DTOs

examples.title: A create input with Omit
examples.prompt: Create users from an input that has no id and no creation time, because the function sets both.
examples.explanation: `NewUser` is `User` without `id` and `createdAt`, so callers pass only what they know. The function adds the rest, and its return type checks that the result is a whole `User`. A caller can't sneak in an id of its own either, because an object literal with an `id` key is an excess property error here. The time comes in as a parameter instead of from the clock, so the output is the same on every run, and a test can pass any time it likes.

examples.title: A list view with Pick
examples.prompt: Turn full users into summaries for a list that shows only ids and names.
examples.explanation: `UserSummary` has just `id` and `name`, with their types copied from `User`. `summarize` builds a new object with those two fields, so the JSON leaves the emails out. Types never remove fields at runtime, though. Because of structural typing, `return user;` would compile too, since a `User` has an `id` and a `name`, and then every email would end up in the JSON. Build the smaller object yourself.

examples.title: A complete table with Record
examples.prompt: List what each role may do, and forget one of the roles.
examples.output: main.ts(3,7): error TS2741: Property 'viewer' is missing in type '{ admin: string[]; editor: string[]; }' but required in type 'Record<Role, string[]>'.
examples.explanation: With a union of literals as its keys, `Record<Role, string[]>` needs every role, and `tsc` names the one that's missing. Add `viewer: ["read"]` and the program prints `read`. The same check protects you later: add `"owner"` to `Role`, and every table typed this way stops compiling until it says what an owner may do. Typed as `Record<string, string[]>`, the incomplete table would compile, and the missing role would only show up as `undefined` when you look it up.

practice.title: Create a task
practice.prompt:
Build the input type for creating tasks from `Task`, and use it to create two tasks.

1. Make `NewTask` the `Task` type without `id`, `done`, and `createdAt`, using `Omit`.
2. Make `createTask` return a `Task`: the input's fields, the given `id`, `done` set to `false`, and `createdAt` set to `now`.
3. Create task 1, `"Write the report"`, at `2026-10-01T09:00:00Z`, and task 2, `"Book the venue"`, at `2026-10-01T09:30:00Z`, and print each with `show`.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests use `createTask` and `NewTask`.

Expected output:

```text
1. Write the report (open, created 2026-10-01T09:00:00Z)
2. Book the venue (open, created 2026-10-01T09:30:00Z)
```

tests.output:
1. Write the report (open, created 2026-10-01T09:00:00Z)
2. Book the venue (open, created 2026-10-01T09:30:00Z)

cases.name: creates a task from just a title
rejects an input that sets done
rejects an input that sets the id

hints: `NewUser` in the first example is built the same way: `Omit` and a union of the keys to leave out.
Spread `input` into a new object between the fields you set yourself: `id` first, then `done` and `createdAt`.
`export type NewTask = Omit<Task, "id" | "done" | "createdAt">;` and `return { id, ...input, done: false, createdAt: now };`

steps.title: Exclude, Extract, and NonNullable

examples.title: Active tickets with Exclude
examples.prompt: Derive the statuses that still need work from all ticket statuses, and say what happens next for each.
examples.output:
new: assign an agent
solved: nothing to do
waiting: follow up in two days
closed: nothing to do
assigned: reply to the customer
examples.explanation: `ActiveStatus` is computed from `TicketStatus`, so the two can't drift apart. `nextStep` only accepts active statuses, and its `switch` handles all three, so every path returns. The type predicate `isActive` does the same filtering on values while the program runs, and it narrows `s`, which is why the call to `nextStep` compiles. Add a status like `"escalated"` to `TicketStatus`, and it becomes active too: `nextStep` stops compiling until it has a case for it.

examples.title: One event type with Extract
examples.prompt: Pick the click events out of a union of UI events, and handle only those.
examples.explanation: `Extract` keeps the members of `UiEvent` that fit `{ type: "click" }`. Only the click member has that `type`, and it comes out whole, with `x` and `y`. You never retype its fields, so a field added to clicks in `UiEvent` reaches `ClickEvent` too. In the loop, `e.type === "click"` narrows `e` to the same member, which is why `describeClick(e)` compiles.

examples.title: Dropping null with NonNullable
examples.prompt: Write a generic compact function that removes null and undefined from an array and keeps everything else, even 0.
examples.explanation: `T` is the element type without the empty values: `string` for the names, `number` for the ports. `NonNullable<T>` in the return type promises that no `null` or `undefined` is left, and the arrow passed to `filter` keeps that promise. It is inferred as a type predicate, so `filter` returns the narrowed array. The arrow compares with `null` and `undefined` instead of testing truthiness, which is why the port `0` survives.

practice.title: Open orders
practice.prompt:
Derive the open order statuses with `Exclude`, and say who to contact when an order is stuck in one.

1. Make `OpenStatus` the `OrderStatus` type without `"delivered"` and `"cancelled"`.
2. Make `escalate` return the contact for each open status: `billing team` for `"pending"`, `warehouse` for `"paid"`, and `carrier support` for `"shipped"`.
3. Keep the loop that prints each stuck order, and keep `export`: hidden type tests use `escalate` and `OpenStatus`.

Expected output:

```text
pending: billing team
paid: warehouse
shipped: carrier support
```

tests.output:
pending: billing team
paid: warehouse
shipped: carrier support

cases.name: keeps pending as an open status

hints: `ActiveStatus` in the first example is derived the same way: `Exclude` and the members to drop.
A `switch` with a `case` for each of the three open statuses returns on every path, so it needs no `default`.

steps.title: ReturnType, Parameters, and Awaited

examples.title: A config type from its loader
examples.prompt: Load a config from a map of environment variables, and name the type of what comes back.
examples.explanation: `loadConfig` has no written return type, so TypeScript infers one from its object literal, and `ReturnType<typeof loadConfig>` gives that inferred type the name `Config`. `describe` can then take a `Config` without anyone writing its fields out. Add a `timeoutMs` field to the object `loadConfig` returns, and `Config` has it at once.

examples.title: Argument lists with Parameters
examples.prompt: Name the message type that sendEmail only writes inline, and queue up calls as argument lists.
examples.output:
to ada@example.com: Your invoice
URGENT to ops@example.com: Disk almost full
examples.explanation: `Parameters` turns the parameter list into a tuple and keeps the names as labels. Indexing the tuple with `[1]` gives the second parameter's type, so the message shape gets a name, `Message`, without being written twice. Each entry in `queue` is a whole argument list, checked against the real parameters, and `sendEmail(...args)` spreads one back into a call.

examples.title: Unwrapping a promise with Awaited
examples.prompt: Name the type an async function resolves to, and use it in a function that isn't async.
examples.explanation: An `async` function always returns a promise, so its `ReturnType` is a `Promise`, as the first bubble shows. `Awaited` takes the value out, which is what `await fetchUser(1)` gives you. `badge` needs a plain `User`, not a promise of one, and the derived type says exactly that. The `await` calls sit at the top level of `main.ts`, which works because the program is an ES module.

practice.title: Derive the invoice type
practice.prompt:
`makeInvoice` already builds invoices. Name their type with `ReturnType`, then format an invoice as text.

1. Make `Invoice` the type that `makeInvoice` returns, derived with `ReturnType` and `typeof`.
2. Make `formatInvoice` return these lines joined with `"\n"`: `Invoice for <customer>`, then one row per line of the invoice, `  <qty> x <description>: $<amount>` with two spaces in front, then `Total: $<total> <currency>`.
3. Write every amount in dollars with 2 decimals.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests use `makeInvoice` and `Invoice`.

Expected output:

```text
Invoice for Ada Lovelace
  2 x Notebook: $9.00
  1 x Fountain pen: $25.99
Total: $34.99 USD
```

tests.output:
Invoice for Ada Lovelace
  2 x Notebook: $9.00
  1 x Fountain pen: $25.99
Total: $34.99 USD

cases.name: has the customer as a string
cases.code:
declare const inv: Invoice;
const c: string = inv.customer;

cases.name: keeps totalCents a number
cases.code:
declare const inv: Invoice;
const t: string = inv.totalCents;

cases.name: has no fields makeInvoice doesn't return

hints: In a type position, `typeof makeInvoice` is the function's type, and `ReturnType` takes it from there, the way `Config` is made in the first example.
Build the rows with `map` over `inv.lines`, put the header in front and the total after, and join them with `"\n"`. `(cents / 100).toFixed(2)` turns cents into dollars.

recap:
- `Partial<T>`, `Required<T>`, and `Readonly<T>` change every property of `T` at once: all optional, all required, or all read-only.
- `Omit<T, K>` and `Pick<T, K>` build smaller types from a bigger one, like a create input or a list item. `Omit` doesn't check its keys, so spell them carefully.
- `Record<K, V>` with a union of literals as `K` must list every member.
- `Exclude`, `Extract`, and `NonNullable` filter a union, member by member.
- `ReturnType<typeof f>`, `Parameters<typeof f>`, and `Awaited<T>` derive types from functions you already wrote, so the types follow the code.
- Types never change values. Pair `Readonly` with `Object.freeze`, and `Pick` with code that copies only the fields you want.
